stories.title: Self-assembling peptide hydrogel SPG-178 effectively prevents postoperative pancreatic fistula compared with polyglycolic acid mesh with fibrin glue in rats
stories.description: Postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF) is a common and potentially life-threatening complication after pancreatectomy. Although various methods have attempted to prevent POPF, none have proven to be fully effective. This study used a rat model to compare the efficacy of a self-assembling peptide hydrogel, SPG-178, in preventing POPF with that of polyglycolic acid mesh combined with fibrin glue (PGA + FG). A rat model of POPF was created by pancreatic transection. The rats were randomly assigned to groups in which the pancreatic stump was untreated (control) or treated with SPG-178 or PGA + FG. The groups were compared based on ascitic amylase levels, macroscopic findings at relaparotomy (saponification and adhesion), and histological examination of the resected specimens. Three days after transection, the mean (± standard deviation) ascitic amylase level was significantly lower in the SPG-178 group (109 ± 58 IU/L) than in the control (283 ± 126 IU/L) and PGA + FG (219 ± 128 IU/L) groups (p < 0.0001). On relaparotomy, saponification around the pancreatic stump and intra-abdominal adhesions were markedly reduced in the SPG-178 group compared with the other groups. Histological analysis also found milder edema, necrosis, hemorrhage, and inflammatory cell infiltration in the SPG-178 group than in the PGA + FG group. SPG-178 demonstrated favorable sealing performance compared with PGA + FG in this rat model. These findings support further preclinical and clinical evaluation of SPG-178 as a novel sealant for preventing postoperative pancreatic fistula.

stories.title: Evolutionary transitions in social organization and the relationship between climate and queen number in ant societies
stories.description: In about one fourth of ant species, multiple queens reproduce within the same colony (‘polygyny’), reducing relatedness and potentially fuelling evolutionary conflicts among colony members. Polygyny is more common at higher altitudes / latitudes in several species, suggesting that cold climates favour multiple queens. We tested this prediction with phylogenetic analyses comparing 263 ant species and modelled the evolutionary pathways between alternative social structures. Queen number was phylogenetically labile, with bidirectional transitions between single and multi-queen species passing through socially polymorphic species (with both types of colonies). Contrary to our predictions, polygyny was not more common at higher latitudes or altitudes. Socially polymorphic species tended to occur in environments with more uniform precipitation throughout the year, and queen number increased towards the tropics. We discuss how multiple queening may be favoured in warm climates due to competitive advantages of faster colony growth and higher genetic diversity. We also call for more studies in tropical regions, as most studies were performed in the northern hemisphere.
